The current opening covers conditional meaning, sufficient/necessary conditions, Group 1 and Group 2. He wants original examples, his selected teaching voice, purposeful visuals, embedded flashcards, and teacher-controlled assignments.

The latest request was to inspect a newly clipped LSAT Lab note, including screenshots, through approximately minute 10 and incorporate its relevant content.

- The supplied Conditional Reasoning HTML remains the **13-part teaching skeleton**. LSAT Lab adds depth and examples of teaching technique; its compressed video order does not replace that skeleton.

- Three difficulty levels were selected previously: beginner, medium, advanced. Timing may supplement medium/advanced work.

## developer

<multi_agent_role>You are an agent in a team of agents collaborating to complete a task.

You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents. All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.

When you provide a response in the final channel, that content is immediately delivered back to your parent agent.
In addition, your final answer may be read by a human, so ensure it is legible.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: NEW_TASK | MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```

# Jay 2 — operating instructions for Codex (ai-os)

Resolve paths from the repository root instead of assuming a saved Mac or Windows absolute path. This is the router: it holds pointers, not knowledge. Read it, then follow the routing map to the right file instead of searching blind. Twin for Claude Code: `CLAUDE.md`.

## Identity and mission

You are **Jay 2**, Joshua's executive assistant. This root is his EA workspace and command center. Joshua is the founder of Aspiring Attorneys and builder of LSAT U (lsatprep.study), a premium LSAT prep platform; he is the product, voice, and content authority. Your job: take operations, admin, drafting, and research off his plate so his time goes to teaching and building. Frame work as decisions and tradeoffs, not basics.

Standing duties, run from here without re-briefing: student operations (transcripts, assignments, follow-ups via `students/`), prospect and consultation correspondence (drafted in his voice, **never auto-sent unless a pre-approved template**), platform actions on lsatprep.study, session-note ingestion from Gmail/Drive, and keeping the wiki ledgers (`tasks`/`hot`/`log`) current so the next session starts oriented.

## Routing map

Paths are relative to the repository root.

Application repositories and dependencies stay outside this Obsidian vault, in sibling `../ai-os-projects/`. Do not create a junction from the vault back into that directory.

## Retrieval order

1. `wiki/hot.md` — current-session narrative and open threads.
2. `wiki/index.md` → the page (teaching knowledge: `corpus/index.md`; a student: their folder). Follow links; there is no semantic search and none is needed at this size.
3. The live system — the final freshness escalation.

**Live systems are authority for operational state; the brain mirrors them:** Cal.com + Google Calendar own sessions scheduled/used, LSAT U Supabase owns homework status/dossier/publish state, Stripe owns payment events, Gmail owns correspondence. On any disagreement, the backend wins. The brain is primary — nothing upstream holds them — for transcripts, teaching notes, judgments, prep briefs, curriculum, product specs, and decisions.

**Do not read the wiki unless the task needs it.** Retrieval costs context every turn. Skip it for: code edits in `../ai-os-projects/lsatu/`; shell/Git/file ops; questions the injected memories already answer; a skill run that names its own inputs; anything mechanical and self-contained. Route to it for: what is X · what did we decide and why · who a student is and where they stand · anything drafted in Joshua's voice for someone else · any decision touching roadmap, pedagogy, or UX.

**LLM Wiki schema:** For knowledge intake, knowledge questions, durable synthesis, and wiki maintenance, follow `system/schema/llm-wiki.md`. Use `ingest` as the single intake entry point; keep sources immutable, compile into existing pages, update the complete fenced catalog in `wiki/index.md`, and append changes to `wiki/log.md`. Preserve domain homes and live-system authority. Mechanical tasks retain the retrieval exceptions above.

**Wiki operations (LLM-wiki pattern):** the LLM writes/maintains `wiki/` and `corpus/`; Joshua sources, explores, asks. Raw sources are immutable — read, never modify. *Ingest:* read the source from `raw/`, discuss takeaways, write/update the pages it touches, update `wiki/index.md`, append to `wiki/log.md` (`## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | Title`); one source at a time, supervised, unless Joshua says batch. *Query:* index first, then pages; file valuable answers back as pages so explorations compound. *Lint:* `second-brain-lint` for contradictions, stale claims, orphans, missing pages.

## Voice

- **No em-dashes, ever.** Joshua never types them; a stray em-dash reads as AI and costs trust.
- **No AI-slop vocabulary** — never "delve," "tapestry," "testament," "demystify," "boasts," "in the realm of," and their kin.
- **Anything a student or prospect will read** routes through `wiki/teaching-voice.md` and is drafted, never sent, unless it is a pre-approved template.
- **LSAT teaching:** use project-owned `lsat-u-voice` and `references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md`; this Joshua-selected standard takes precedence over older vendor voice blends.
- **When an outbound message is authorized**, preserve the draft's paragraph breaks, list lines, and intentional spacing. After sending, compare the recipient-facing rendering with the draft and confirm exactly one copy landed. Report any mismatch; never resend automatically.
- **Lead with your recommendation, not a menu.** Be decisive; don't over-hedge.
- **Any prompt Joshua will paste elsewhere** goes inside a fenced code block, never inline prose.

Everything is a skill — **there are no slash commands** (decided 2026-07-17: one kind, one home, one activation path). The catalog at `skills/` and `agents/` is inert storage; nothing auto-loads. Active in this root. Run `pickup` only when Joshua explicitly asks for it. Do not run it automatically at session start. Use `wrapup` at the end of substantive sessions:

| Skill | Use it when |
|---|---|
| `pickup` / `wrapup` | `pickup` only on Joshua's explicit request / `wrapup` at session end (wrapup persists to the wiki ledgers) |

## Guardrails

- **95% rule.** Make no changes until you are 95% confident what Joshua wants. Ask until you are.
- **Lovable credits require confirmation.** Never take an action that spends or may spend Lovable credits without Joshua's explicit confirmation immediately before the action. Do not infer approval from a broader request to fix, build, deploy, or continue. Free Lovable controls and direct deployment paths may be used without this credit-spend confirmation.
- **Lovable Cloud deploys through Lovable.** LSAT U currently uses a Lovable Cloud-managed backend. Deploy its Edge Functions through the Lovable agent, not the Supabase CLI, unless the backend has first been migrated to a separately managed Supabase project. Confirm this route with Joshua before starting a Lovable deployment.
- **Root stays thin.** Don't accumulate files at the root; work products go to their homes (wiki, students, corpus, projects). Anything left at root gets filed before the session ends.
- **Delegate bulk work.** Exploration or analysis spanning 3+ files goes to a sub-agent that returns summaries, not file dumps.
- **Shell ergonomics.** Run one command per call — chained `cmd; cmd` and `rm -rf X && clone Y` forms trip permission denials that the split commands would not. Never poll with `sleep`. Use backgrounded execution for anything slow, and raise the timeout explicitly for known-slow ops (large moves, typecheck-gated pushes, full verify runs) rather than eating the default.
- **Search before creating.** One authoritative page per subject — update it, don't grow a parallel truth. `wiki/index.md` catalogs every page and updates on every ingest.
- **Preserve provenance and source hashes.** Never move, delete, or modify a migration source root — copy and hash-verify. Never follow a source symlink outside its registered root.
- **Conflicts stay explicit until adjudicated** — never silently overwrite one source generation with another.
- **Automation writes only generated files or fenced generated sections,** through compare-and-swap.
- **Obey nested instruction files** — they win over broader ones for their subtree. LSATU's recovered `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` are inviolate: never regenerate them without Joshua's explicit approval.
- **Memory = native automemory.** "Remember that…" writes one fact per file to the native store; `MEMORY.md` indexes it. This file is the rules; memory is learned facts — never mix them. Transcripts and raw captures never auto-promote.
- **Append meaningful system changes** to `wiki/log.md`; log locked decisions to `decisions/log.md`.

- Begin at the Git-root `AGENTS.md` and follow directory-scoped instruction files toward the working path; the nearest file wins for its subtree.
- Keep root instructions inside the runtime byte budget. Move narrow rules to the narrowest owning directory rather than growing this file.

- Never have Claude and Codex editing the same file at once; pass work between them by session handoff (summarize → clear → paste). At ~250k tokens, hand off rather than riding autocompact.

Do not commit/publish.\\r\\n---\\r\\ntype: synthesis\\r\\nsubject: LSAT teaching voice standard\\r\\ncreated: 2026-10-02\\r\\nupdated: 2026-10-03\\r\\naliases: [LSAT voice reference, Conditional transcription writing standard]\\r\\ntags: [lsat-u, voice, pedagogy, writing]\\r\\nsources:\\r\\n  - ../wiki/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# LSAT teaching: make the reasoning sound like someone thinking\\r\\n\\r\\n**This is Joshua\'s selected reference for writing LSAT teaching material.** Use it for bootcamp lessons, lecture notes, explanations, guided examples, drills, flashcards, quizzes, reference pages, and instructional feedback. It develops the teaching-content register in [the canonical teaching voice](../wiki/teaching-voice.md). That document still governs correspondence and marketing in their own registers.\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua selected the supplied **Conditional Reasoning** transcription on 2026-10-02 because of its writing, tone, word choice, cadence, point of view, progression, and depth. The goal is to reproduce those qualities closely through original wording and examples. The central quality is patient, conversational reasoning that the reader can follow and eventually perform.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source is a calibration example. This guide separates **observed features** from **instructions for our material**. A source habit is not automatically a rule, a research finding, or permission to import a topic. Matching the voice does not require repeating the same metaphors, anecdotes, exercise sentences, or personal claims.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Find the part you need\\r\\n\\r\\n- [The evidence and coverage](#the-evidence-and-coverage)\\r\\n- [The voice in one original passage](#the-voice-in-one-original-passage)\\r\\n- [How the teacher relates to the reader](#how-the-teacher-relates-to-the-reader)\\r\\n- [Sentence length and spoken cadence](#sentence-length-and-spoken-cadence)\\r\\n- [Word choice and useful verbal habits](#word-choice-and-useful-verbal-habits)\\r\\n- [Questions that make the reader think](#questions-that-make-the-reader-think)\\r\\n- [Transitions, repetition, metaphor, and emphasis](#transitions-explain-why-the-next-move-follows)\\r\\n- [The complete source progression and depth](#the-complete-source-progression-and-depth)\\r\\n- [What to carry into the Conditional Bootcamp](#what-to-carry-into-the-conditional-bootcamp)\\r\\n- [Accuracy and method boundaries](#accuracy-and-method-boundaries)\\r\\n- [Calibration examples and review](#calibration-examples-for-different-lsat-surfaces)\\r\\n- [A reusable writing brief](#a-reusable-writing-brief)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The evidence and coverage\\r\\n\\r\\nThe [source summary](../wiki/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md) identifies the [preserved HTML](../raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/conditional_reasoning_transcription.html), [provenance](../raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/PROVENANCE.md), and SHA-256. Every supplied section, FAQ entry, table, worked diagram, and drill item was read. HTML line references below refer to that unchanged archived file.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe document has six main sections and six subordinate headings. It ends with six basic drill items and an answer-key reference. One line is explicitly marked partially obscured. The answer key is not supplied. This analysis covers the entire attachment; it cannot reconstruct the missing line or establish the contents of the larger chapter.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe HTML says its formatting was adjusted. We can examine what a pause, table, side note, or separated example does for learning. We cannot claim its font, spacing, color, or CSS exactly reproduces the original publication. No author is identified in the file. The exercise wording attributed to Shakespeare is separate from the narrator\'s teaching voice.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The voice in one original passage\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following is a new calibration passage. Its example was created for this guide; it is not a source quotation or an approved bootcamp page.\\r\\n\\r\\n> A conditional tells us that if one thing is true, something else has to be true too.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Suppose a shop has this rule: **Every parcel with a blue sticker has been inspected.**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> You pick up a parcel with a blue sticker. What do you know about it?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> It has been inspected. The rule covers every parcel with that sticker, including the one in your hand. A blue-sticker parcel that hadn\'t been inspected would break the rule.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Now turn the parcel over. It has an inspection stamp, but you can\'t see a blue sticker. Does it have to have one?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We don\'t know. The rule tells us something about parcels with blue stickers. It doesn\'t tell us that every inspected parcel gets a sticker.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> That\'s the distinction we need: **what the sentence makes certain, and what it leaves open.**\\r\\n\\r\\nNotice the opening definition before the example, the small prediction, the explanation connecting the rule to the case, and the change in what the reader is given. The last sentence names a distinction the reader has just seen. The passage has a conversational rhythm because it follows a person\'s thoughts. Casual vocabulary alone would not accomplish that.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn an interactive lesson, pause after the first question and again after the inspection-stamp question. Reveal each explanation after the learner has had an opportunity to answer. The printed passage shows the whole progression for calibration.\\r\\n\\r\\n## How the teacher relates to the reader\\r\\n\\r\\n### The reader is beside the teacher\\r\\n\\r\\nThe narrator talks directly to someone doing the work. “Let\'s,” “you,” and “we” keep the reader involved. The writing seldom steps back to describe what students generally do. It asks this reader to notice, try, decide, or check something now.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe reader is treated as capable of understanding ordinary meaning. The teacher supplies support when a technical step is new. In the opening, the source first gives the literal relationship, then asks the reader to take its certainty seriously. Later, it encourages a guess before revealing the contrapositive. These are expectations of participation, not claims that everything should feel easy.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For our writing:** speak to the reader without making their intelligence the subject. Do not copy a line such as “Because you\'re a thinking human.” Give them a manageable question and the information to answer it. If they miss it, explain the precise move that went wrong.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Confidence lives in the reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source is decisive about a valid consequence. It also says “We don\'t know” when the information cannot settle a question. These two kinds of confidence belong together. Clear teaching can be certain about the limits of what is known.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe teacher does not apologize for asking the reader to think. The explanation makes the request reasonable. In the FAQ, the narrator acknowledges early mistakes and explains the value of practicing anyway. The tone combines patience with a specific demand: attempt the question, write the diagram, inspect the error.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For our writing:** state the consequence plainly and show why. Preserve legitimate uncertainty. Avoid changing a logical “could” into “must” to make the prose sound stronger. Avoid guarantees about learning outcomes, timing, or score changes unless we have evidence.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Warmth points at the work\\r\\n\\r\\nEncouragement is usually tied to an action. The reader can look back at the lesson, make a provisional attempt, learn from a wrong translation, or build confidence by checking work. The warmth comes from useful help and a teacher who expects progress.\\r\\n\\r\\nUseful form:\\r\\n\\r\\n> If the direction felt unclear, read the statement back in ordinary English. What does it say you need? Keep that complete idea in your diagram.\\r\\n\\r\\nWeak form:\\r\\n\\r\\n> You\'ve got this! Conditionals are easy once you know the trick!\\r\\n\\r\\nThe weak version offers reassurance without a way forward and minimizes the actual difficulty.\\r\\n\\r\\n### “I,” “we,” and “you” have different jobs\\r\\n\\r\\n| Pronoun | What it does in the source | Use in our material |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| **You** | Gives the reader an action or asks for a decision. | “Try the sentence in the other direction. Does it still say the same thing?” |\\r\\n| **We / let\'s** | Makes the explanation a shared investigation. | “Let\'s keep the rule and change the fact.” |\\r\\n| **I**, thinking aloud | Shows the teacher making a decision: noticing an indicator, identifying its target, placing a label. | “I see …7622 tokens truncated… one definition and one answer. It may need a literal explanation, a familiar example, a variation, a pause, a mistaken interpretation, a correction, and a short practice task.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor Group 1, that could become several small lessons: recognizing “if,” locating the complete if-clause, reading an if-clause at the end of the sentence, handling a universal expression, and checking that the diagram preserves the meaning. Group 2 deserves its own development. Do not flatten all expressions into a word table and assume coverage.\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep micro-assignments possible. A student who needs “only if” should be able to receive that work without repeating every beginner concept. A general assignment can connect the lessons into a full sequence. Beginner, medium, and advanced describe teacher-assigned work; optional timing belongs to medium and advanced practice after accuracy is established.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Preserve the real indicator groups\\r\\n\\r\\nThe current reviewed opening materials use:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Group 1:** if, when, where, all, the only, every, any.\\r\\n- **Group 2:** only, only if, only when, only where, always, requires, must.\\r\\n\\r\\nSee the [reviewed opening source constraints](../brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/notebooklm-opening-assets/sufficient-necessary-infographic-prompt.txt). These lists are current project teaching groups, not a claim that every occurrence of each word mechanically diagrammed in isolation has the same function. The supplied source\'s two families have different members. Do not merge inventories without checking Joshua\'s notes and scope.\\r\\n\\r\\n“The only” especially requires its complete grammatical target. The only people admitted are members means **Admitted → Member**. Only members are admitted means the same relationship, reached through a different expression. The lesson must show the meaning rather than encourage a next-word shortcut.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Preserve Joshua\'s five steps\\r\\n\\r\\nIn [Sandra\'s 2026-09-28 transcript](../students/sandra/transcript-downloads/2026-09-28-sandra-notes-by-gemini.md), at 00:43:22, Joshua gives this sequence: identify the indicator; label the two ideas; apply the left/right rule; find the contrapositive; say it back in English. This is a summary of his sequence, not a verbatim quotation. At 00:37:08, he stresses understanding and reading the diagram rather than retaining bare letters.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe supplied source has four construction steps. Do not quietly replace Joshua\'s five with those four, or claim a shortened opening exercise has taught all five. In a gradual introduction, teach the operations whose prerequisites have been established and identify the full contrapositive step when that lesson is reached. Keep English readback visible as a meaning check throughout.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Carry these improvements forward\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Define before demonstrating.** Start by explaining what a conditional says. Let the example make the definition concrete.\\r\\n2. **Explain the purpose through a decision.** Show how direction changes the conclusion the learner may draw. Avoid unsupported prevalence statistics.\\r\\n3. **Keep one relationship stable while changing the view.** Ordinary sentence, case fact, roles, wording variation, and diagram should fit together.\\r\\n4. **Make each pause a useful thinking task.** Ask for a prediction or explanation, then reveal the reason.\\r\\n5. **Show a mistake being detected.** A wrong arrow becomes understandable when its English meaning fails the original sentence.\\r\\n6. **Teach the target before the placement shortcut becomes a habit.** Complete ideas and their qualifications matter.\\r\\n7. **Explain why the drill exists.** The learner should know what ability they are practicing.\\r\\n8. **Use fresh practice.** Worked examples teach the method; new items show whether the method transfers.\\r\\n9. **Give practical objections an answer.** Time, confidence, notation, and when to write deserve specific guidance.\\r\\n10. **Keep each operation behind its prerequisites.** Under the 2026-10-03 sequence, conceptual contraposition follows both condition roles and families, and precedes notation. Chains, Groups 3/4 and quantities still receive later development. The source does not contain those complete later curricula.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Accuracy and method boundaries\\r\\n\\r\\nWriting that sounds like the source must still preserve correct logic and Joshua\'s chosen method.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Source simplification or context | Boundary for our material |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| “Ignore the conditional” when sufficient is absent or necessary is present. | For this one rule and fact, no new conclusion about the other condition follows. The rule remains available for later facts and chains. Never teach that it disappears. |\\r\\n| Necessary has to happen “at some point.” | A conditional is not necessarily a time sequence or causal claim. Prefer “has to be true if the sufficient condition is true.” |\\r\\n| The original and contrapositive are “all you know.” | The central warning is against an unsupported reverse or inverse. Equivalent formulations and other supplied rules still matter. State the immediate inference limits precisely. |\\r\\n| Required words are described as obligations. | Preserve modality. “Interviewees must bring ID” can assert an obligation, not prove compliance. Diagram the stated requirement unless the facts establish compliance. |\\r\\n| Indicator usually comes before target. | Read its full grammatical target. Targets can precede the indicator, and familiar words can serve other roles in context. |\\r\\n| Shorten conditions to one or two letters, never more than four. | Joshua\'s clear condensed labels govern. Keep negation, scope, qualifiers, and readability. A short label that loses meaning is not an improvement. |\\r\\n| Try a personalized sufficient guess. | Compare with the whole ordinary meaning and look for a counterexample. A feeling that an arrow is plausible is not enough. |\\r\\n| Original and contrapositive training. | Explain why a drill requires explicit work and when test-day practice may differ. Do not turn a training requirement into a universal performance rule. |\\r\\n| “Always” is in a necessary-family teaching list. | Establish the sentence\'s subject and relationship. It is not a universal instruction to place the next word on the right. |\\r\\n| Confidence guarantees the diagram is correct. | Confidence can grow from practice, but correctness rests on preserving meaning and valid reasoning. Provide checks. |\\r\\n| Timing and learning claims are absolute. | Treat them as the author\'s advice unless independently supported. Give a practical explanation without invented evidence. |\\r\\n| References to Logic Games, a book, page 148, or named source tools. | Preserve the teaching function only where our course has an actual equivalent. Do not import obsolete or unavailable context. |\\r\\n| A theme makes a drill memorable. | Keep each sentence logically interpretable and its answer reviewed. Novelty must not obscure the condition or require untaught knowledge. |\\r\\n\\r\\nFor the parcel example, three possible cases distinguish the permitted relationship from an invalid reverse:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Blue sticker and inspected: fits the rule.\\r\\n- Inspected without a blue sticker: also fits the rule.\\r\\n- Blue sticker without inspection: breaks the rule.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe rule does not itself say any such parcel exists. Examples of possible cases illustrate consistency, not existence claims. This distinction matters when moving from individual facts to general rules.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Calibration examples for different LSAT surfaces\\r\\n\\r\\nAll examples below are original drafts for this reference. They demonstrate writing mechanisms; they are not assigned work or approved curriculum.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Explain sufficient and necessary without rushing\\r\\n\\r\\n> Every parcel with a blue sticker has been inspected.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Suppose yours has a blue sticker. That\'s enough to know it has been inspected. You don\'t need another fact about the parcel. The rule has already told you what must be true of every parcel with that sticker.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We call the blue sticker the **sufficient condition**. Sufficient means enough. Here, enough to establish inspection under this rule.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Inspection is the **necessary condition**. A blue-sticker parcel has to meet that requirement. Otherwise it would be an exception to a rule that allows no exceptions.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Now suppose a parcel has been inspected. Does it have to have a blue sticker?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We still don\'t know. Inspection was required for the blue-sticker parcels. The shop never said those were the only parcels it inspected.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis returns to meaning at every term. The example does not assert why the shop uses stickers or when they are applied. Those extra facts are unnecessary.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Teach a necessary expression through its whole meaning\\r\\n\\r\\n> Editing this newsletter requires an account.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> What does the sentence say the editor needs? An account. Keep that complete idea on the required side of the relationship:\\r\\n>\\r\\n> **Edits this newsletter → Has an account**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Read it back: if someone edits this newsletter, they have an account. That matches the sentence.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Try the reverse. If someone has an account, do they necessarily edit the newsletter? The sentence hasn\'t told us that. An account could belong to someone who only reads it.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe final possible counterexample is introduced as something consistent with the sentence, not an asserted fact about this system. Technical placement has a semantic reason.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Give a flashcard a reasoning task\\r\\n\\r\\n**Front**\\r\\n\\r\\n> Every package in Locker 4 has been scanned. A package has been scanned. Must it be in Locker 4? Why?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Back**\\r\\n\\r\\n> No. The rule tells us about packages already in Locker 4. It doesn\'t say every scanned package goes there.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is more useful than a card that only asks “Necessary condition = which side?” Keep simple recall cards when recall is the actual skill; do not mistake that for complete reasoning practice.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Make feedback identify the missed connection\\r\\n\\r\\n> You used the sentence in the reverse direction. “Only registered visitors enter the archive” requires registration for entry. It hasn\'t said every registered visitor enters. Read the diagram as **Enters → Registered** and compare it with the sentence.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe feedback names the mistake, shows the relevant meaning, and gives a repair. It avoids generic praise, mockery, and labels such as “weak reasoning.”\\r\\n\\r\\n### Explain an ordinary learning objection\\r\\n\\r\\n> “I understood the sentence. Why write it down?”\\r\\n>\\r\\n> With one short rule, you may not need to. When a passage gives you several relationships, a diagram lets you compare them without rereading the wording each time. In this exercise, write the relationship so we can check that you kept its direction and complete ideas.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe answer gives a decision criterion and distinguishes the purpose of this exercise from a blanket rule about every test question.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Transfer the voice to another LSAT topic\\r\\n\\r\\n> A conclusion is the claim the author is asking you to accept. The other statements are supposed to support it.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Nora says, “The library should stay open later because every evening seat was taken this week.” What is she trying to persuade us of?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> That the library should stay open later. The full seats are her reason. She expects that reason to support the proposed change.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> You don\'t have to agree with her. First, separate what she wants you to accept from what she gives you in support.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe same mechanism works outside conditionals: definition, small example, question, explanation, and a useful boundary. No conditional topic has been imported into the conclusion lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Revise the draft in a useful order\\r\\n\\r\\n### First, check the reasoning and scope\\r\\n\\r\\nList what is given, what follows, and why. Try to construct a case that satisfies the given information but makes the proposed conclusion false. If that case is possible, revise the logic before polishing the voice. Check modality, negation, quantifier scope, and whether the learner has actually been taught every required operation.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor a rewrite, preserve Joshua\'s established method and explicit lesson scope. The new reference governs delivery. It does not authorize removing content that students need or adding source topics the current assignment does not cover.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Then, check the learner\'s experience\\r\\n\\r\\nRead as someone who has never seen the notation. Can they tell what the concept is? Can they answer the first question with what the page has taught? Does each new term refer to an idea they have seen? Does the page tell them why the correct answer follows?\\r\\n\\r\\nPut the explanation beside the point where it is needed. Do not rely on an interaction to imply a distinction the prose never explains. A student who cannot use the animation must still be able to learn from the text.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Then, listen to the voice\\r\\n\\r\\nRead aloud at an ordinary teaching pace. Replace stiff phrasing with the words the teacher would naturally use. Keep the intermediate thoughts. Vary sentence length where the task changes. Remove repeated catchphrases, inflated enthusiasm, branded metaphors, and irrelevant asides.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not repair generic prose by scattering “Cool,” “Let\'s,” or “That\'s it” through it. Repair the missing reasoning, the abrupt transition, or the abstract example.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Finally, verify the student surface\\r\\n\\r\\nCheck the actual prompt, answer state, labels, buttons, diagrams, and explanations. A good note can be undermined by a shell that exposes internal planning or reveals the answer too soon. Preview desktop and mobile when the interface changes. Keep the instructor\'s planning map separate from what the learner sees.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Use this rubric before handing over LSAT writing\\r\\n\\r\\nScore each dimension from 0 to 2: **0** absent or misleading; **1** partly present but needing revision; **2** clear and usable. This is an editorial tool, not a validated learning measure. A logical error or scope violation requires revision regardless of the total.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Dimension | What a strong draft does |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| **Ordinary meaning** | Defines the idea in language the reader can understand before notation. |\\r\\n| **Concrete anchor** | Uses an original, small, unambiguous situation and states needed assumptions. |\\r\\n| **Visible reasoning** | Shows the intermediate connection instead of asserting a result. |\\r\\n| **Point of view** | Keeps the reader involved; uses teacher narration purposefully. |\\r\\n| **Cadence** | Gives complex thoughts room and short conclusions a clear place to land. |\\r\\n| **Vocabulary** | Keeps useful technical terms, explains them, and avoids internal jargon. |\\r\\n| **Questions and pauses** | Asks a genuine decision and gives an appropriate chance to answer. |\\r\\n| **Boundaries** | Shows what the information leaves open and why a tempting move fails. |\\r\\n| **Progression** | Each operation has a prerequisite, a reason to appear, and adequate practice. |\\r\\n| **Transfer** | Fresh questions require the taught skill, with reasoned feedback. |\\r\\n| **Tone and warmth** | Expects effort, supports the next action, and never mocks uncertainty. |\\r\\n| **Presentation** | Examples, comparisons, notation, and interactions clarify the reasoning. |\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not treat a high total as proof of an identical voice. Use the original source and Joshua\'s response to calibrate the subjective feel. His concrete corrections override a score.\\r\\n\\r\\n## A reusable writing brief\\r\\n\\r\\nUse this when giving another writer or agent the task. Supply the actual source, lesson scope, prerequisite knowledge, and approved method along with it.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nWrite this LSAT material in Joshua\'s selected teaching voice.\\r\\nRead wiki/teaching-voice.md, references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md,\\r\\nand wiki/COPY-CORRECTIONS.md before drafting.\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep the reader beside the teacher. Start with the ordinary meaning of\\r\\nthe idea, then make it concrete with an original, intuitive example.\\r\\nShow each small inference in natural language. Ask the question a learner\\r\\nwould actually need to answer here. When the question is practice, leave\\r\\nroom for an attempt before revealing the reasoning.\\r\\n\\r\\nVary sentence length by purpose. Let explanations breathe and use short\\r\\nsentences to settle a consequence or a limit. Use contractions naturally.\\r\\nTeach the technical term when there is a clear idea to attach it to.\\r\\nRepeat an anchor only when the repetition changes the learner\'s view.\\r\\nShow a tempting mistake and how to detect it when that distinction matters.\\r\\n\\r\\nPreserve Joshua\'s method, the exact logical strength, complete conditions,\\r\\nand the selected topic scope. Give fresh practice with explained answers.\\r\\nDo not copy the reference\'s examples, jokes, personal claims, or procedural\\r\\ncounts. No em dashes, hype, invented evidence, internal stage language,\\r\\nor decorative catchphrases. Light humor is optional and must help the lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\nRead the result aloud, check every inference, and review the student-facing\\r\\nprompt and answer states. If the reader cannot hear why the next thought\\r\\nfollows, revise the explanation before polishing the surface.\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## Keep this reference current\\r\\n\\r\\nThis file is the detailed method reference, not a second canonical brand voice. Taylor Menu\n\nDigital Commons @ USF > College of Arts and Sciences > Psychology > Faculty Publications > 1767\n\n## Psychology Faculty Publications\n\n\xa0\n\n# The Shuffling of Mathematics Practice Problems Boosts Learning\n\n  * Doug Rohrer, University of South FloridaFollow\n  * Kelli M. Taylor, University of South Florida\n\n## Document Type\n\nArticle\n\n## Publication Date\n\n11-2007\n\n## Keywords\n\nMathematics, Practice, Distribute, Mass, Block, Mix, Interleave, Spacing\n\n## Digital Object Identifier (DOI)\n\nhttps://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9015-8\n\n## Abstract\n\nIn most mathematics textbooks, each set of practice problems is comprised almost entirely of problems corresponding to the immediately previous lesson. By contrast, in a small number of textbooks, the practice problems are systematically shuffled so that each practice set includes a variety of problems drawn from many previous lessons. The standard and shuffled formats differ in two critical ways, and each was the focus of an experiment reported here. In Experiment 1, college students learned to solve one kind of problem, and subsequent practice problems were either massed in a single session (as in the standard format) or spaced across multiple sessions (as in the shuffled format). When tested 1 week later, performance was much greater after spaced practice. In Experiment 2, students first learned to solve multiple types of problems, and practice problems were either blocked by type (as in the standard format) or randomly mixed (as in the shuffled format). When tested 1 week later, performance was vastly superior after mixed practice. Thus, the results of both experiments favored the shuffled format over the standard format.\n\n## Was this content written or created while at USF?\n\nYes\n\n## Citation / Publisher Attribution\n\nInstructional Science, v. 35, issue 6, p. 481-498\n\n## Scholar Commons Citation\n\nRohrer, Doug and Taylor, Kelli M., "The Shuffling of Mathematics Practice Problems Boosts Learning" (2007). ## assistant

Reviewed actual Intro to LR source, conditional work order, and selected voice standard. Sent Astra these implementation priorities:

- Next/Back should name the destination; completion remains explicit at the lesson’s end.
- Follow explanation → worked example → partially supported attempt → fresh application.
- Use clause selection, diagram repair, counterexample checks, and wording comparisons.
- Flashcards should prompt recall and reasoning before revealing.
- Correct the specific misconception in feedback.
- Mix Group 1/2 discrimination only after teaching both.

Evidence supports these design choices, without establishing LSAT-specific outcomes: [retrieval practice](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21252317/), [fading with self-explanation](https://experts.azregents.edu/en/publications/transitioning-from-studying-examples-to-solving-problems-effects-/), [corrective feedback](https://psychnet.wustl.edu/memory/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Butler-Roediger-2008_MemCog.pdf), and [interleaved practice](https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/psy_facpub/1767/).

Actual Intro LR route: `http://127.0.0.1:8097/bootcamp/intro-to-lr/lessons/notes/three-parts-lr-question`. It is gated; no dedicated development preview was found.

No files changed. Ready for post-build teaching/retention review.

Read-only research and source comparison for the Conditional Bootcamp opening through Group 2. Recommendations were sent to the Astra builder before implementation. This record does not establish completed implementation or student learning outcomes.\n+\n+## What was inspected\n+\n+Application root: `C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp`.\n+\n+- `AGENTS.md`, `src/App.tsx` and `src/pages/IntroToLrBootcamp.tsx`: actual Intro to LR registration and gate.\n+- `src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/content/introToLrPath.ts`: named, ordered lesson and drill destinations.\n+- `src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/modules/lessons/notes/IntroNotesShell.tsx`: contained reading canvas, local contents navigation, route-change scrolling, previous/next destination titles and descriptions, and completion callback on the next link.\n+- `src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/modules/lessons/notes/IntroLessonPage.tsx`: concept-specific tools embedded in notes, including anatomy scanning, role labeling, support checks and indicator quizzes.\n+- `src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/modules/lessons/introGuidedSequence.ts`: note, checkpoint, drill and practice sequencing. This older guided sequence is contextual evidence; it does not supersede the current route map.\n+- `2026-10-03-claude-pages-build-spec.md` and `references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md`: preserved 13-part progression, novice explanations, source boundaries, state/navigation requirements and selected teaching voice.\n+\n+Actual reference route: `http://127.0.0.1:8097/bootcamp/intro-to-lr/lessons/notes/three-parts-lr-question`. Subsequent note routes include `so-an-argument`, `premises` and `conclusions`. No dedicated Intro to LR development preview was found. The parent opened the actual route and reported **Not assigned yet**. The reference comparison is therefore **source-only**; no visual inspection of the reference lesson itself was established.\n+\n+## Transfer the teaching decisions, not every shell behavior\n+\n+Transfer meaningful Next/Back destination titles, a focused reading canvas, revisitable contents, and an explanation followed by a small relevant action. Keep formative choices and card states when returning within the mounted unit. Give the new page heading predictable focus. A new page should introduce a manageable reasoning demand rather than merely cut a long paragraph at an arbitrary point.\n+\n+Do not transfer IntroNotesShell's completion-on-next behavior to ordinary conditional page flips. The conditional work order requires explicit lesson-read action at the appropriate end. Its animated hero, repeated effects and generic start-card copy are not requirements. Motion should clarify direction, grouping or a learner's action; the static state must teach the same idea.\n+\n+Useful interaction sequence: show a complete worked example; ask the learner to select the complete condition in a fresh sentence; ask them to repair a reversed diagram and read it back; then give a fresh independent application. Compare equivalent wording while holding the relationship stable. Ask which possible case would break the rule after the relevant inference limits have been taught. Do not introduce transformations or notation before their prerequisite lesson.\n+\n+For cards, ask for meaning or a reason before the learner flips. Reveal the correct reasoning, allow reflip, and preserve stable card position. Card familiarity and page navigation are not assessed mastery. After both indicator families are taught, mix `if` with `only if` and `only` with `the only` so the lesson heading cannot supply the answer. Feedback should name the precise target or direction mistake and show its repair.\n+\n+## Evidence used and what it can support\n+\n+- **Retrieval:** [Karpicke and Blunt, 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21252317/) studied retrieval practice with science material, including conceptual questions. Design inference: invite an actual attempt before showing an answer. It does not show that clicking a flip control by itself improves conditional reasoning.\n+- **Fading and self-explanation:** [Atkinson, Renkl and Merrill, 2003](https://experts.azregents.edu/en/publications/transitioning-from-studying-examples-to-solving-problems-effects-/) reports two experiments combining fading of worked steps with prompts about the underlying principle. Design inference: gradually remove help while retaining a meaningful question about why the direction follows. Fading alone does not establish broad transfer.\n+- **Corrective feedback:** [Butler and Roediger, 2008, author-hosted paper](https://psychnet.wustl.edu/memory/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Butler-Roediger-2008_MemCog.pdf) examines feedback after multiple-choice testing and the risk of learning wrong alternatives. Design inference: explain why the selected wrong answer fails and provide the correct relationship; a color change alone is inadequate teaching.\n+- **Mixed practice:** [Rohrer and Taylor, 2007, university publication record](https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/psy_facpub/1767/) reports mathematics experiments involving spaced and mixed practice. Design inference: after initial teaching, mix confusable conditional formulations so learners must choose the appropriate interpretation. This is not direct evidence about LSAT instruction.\n+- **Instructional synthesis:** [IES, Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/practiceguide/1) recommends worked-example/problem alternation, integrating concrete and abstract representations, combining verbal and graphical explanations, and retrieval and spacing. These support purposeful diagrams and repeated reasoning opportunities. Same-session revisiting is not evidence of a longitudinal spaced-review system.\n+\n+No retention percentage, score gain, optimal pacing interval or guaranteed outcome is claimed. These are bounded design inferences from general learning research. Authenticated student persistence, production behavior and learning effectiveness were not evaluated by this review.\n+\n+## Post-build teaching and retention pass\n+\n+Pending. No implementation findings or approval are claimed before the builder's changes are reviewed.\n*** End Patch"));

true)}>{option}</button>)}</div></fieldset>\\r\\n    <div className=\\"cr-control-row\\"><button type=\\"button\\" className=\\"cr-primary\\" disabled={original === null || contra === null} aria-label={`Check both diagrams for item ${number}`} onClick={() => setChecked(true)}>Check both diagrams</button><button type=\\"button\\" className=\\"cr-reset\\" onClick={reset}>Try item {number} again</button></div>\\r\\n    <div role=\\"status\\">{checked && <div className={`cr-feedback ${correct ? \'cr-correct\' : \'cr-revise\'}`}><strong>{correct ? \'Both diagrams are correct.\' : \'Review the relationship.\'}</strong><p>{original === item.originalPosition ? \'Your original preserves the direction.\' : \'Your original changes the direction or negates conditions the sentence did not negate.\'} {contra === item.contraPosition ? \'Your contrapositive reverses and negates both complete conditions.\' : \'Your contrapositive must start from the missing requirement and rule out the sufficient condition.\'}</p><p>{item.why}</p><p className=\\"cr-answer-key\\">Original: {item.leftCode} → {item.rightCode}<br/>Contrapositive: ~{item.rightCode} → ~{item.leftCode}</p><p>Read the original: {item.readback}</p><p>Read its contrapositive: {item.contraReadback}</p></div>}</div>\\r\\n  </div>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nexport function conditionalReferenceContent() {\\r\\n  return <div className=\\"cr-sequence\\">\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={1} label=\\"Start with meaning\\" title=\\"What does a conditional tell you?\\">\\r\\n      <p>A <strong>condition</strong> is an idea that can be true or false. An order has been packed. A guest has a ticket. We can ask whether either condition holds in a particular case.</p>\\r\\n      <p>A <strong>conditional statement</strong> tells us that if one condition is true, another has to be true too. It gives us a rule we can use, even before we know whether either condition is true in a particular case.</p>\\r\\n      <p className=\\"co-if-inline\\">We aren\'t saying the first condition happened. We\'re asking what would follow <strong>if</strong> it did.</p>\\r\\n      <HypotheticalFigure/>\\r\\n      <h3>Why learn this?</h3><p>On the LSAT, you need to distinguish what the information proves from what it leaves open. A conditional rule can help you prove a conclusion. An argument can also misuse the rule and reach a conclusion it hasn\'t proved. We\'ll practice telling those apart.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Let\'s read one rule.</p><blockquote>{orderRule}</blockquote>\\r\\n      <p>For this rule, the ready label makes packing certain. A ready order that hasn\'t been packed would break the stated relationship. That\'s what we mean by a <strong>guarantee</strong> here.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Compare that with “Ready orders are usually packed.” Usually allows an exception. Our if/then rule doesn\'t. We are working with the rule as given; we aren\'t claiming that every shop in real life follows it.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Does the rule itself tell us that an actual order is marked ready?\\" options={[\'Yes, at least one order is marked ready.\', \'No, it tells us what would follow if an order were marked ready.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'You added a case fact. The rule connects the conditions but has not reported an order with that label.\', \'The imagined ready order lets us understand the rule. We need a separate fact to establish that an actual order has the label.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>Now let\'s take the two conditions one at a time.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={2} label=\\"Sufficient means enough\\" title=\\"One condition gives you enough\\">\\r\\n      <blockquote>{orderRule}</blockquote><p>The <strong>if-part</strong> is the <strong>sufficient condition</strong>. Sufficient means enough. Knowing an order is marked ready is enough, under this rule, to know it has been packed.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-role-exhibit\\"><span>Sufficient</span><strong>Marked ready for pickup</strong><p>Enough to establish packing</p></div>\\r\\n      <p>The ready label might be present. It might not be. The rule hasn\'t settled that question for every order.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Order D isn\'t marked ready. Could it still have been packed?\\" options={[\'Yes. Packing is still possible.\', \'No. Without the label, packing is impossible.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'D could be packed without the label. It could also be unpacked. Neither case creates a ready order that is unpacked, so the rule leaves packing open.\', \'You made the ready label the only way to have packing. The sentence gives one condition that establishes packing; it has not excluded other packed orders.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>Now suppose a fact gives us the sufficient condition. That is when we can <strong>use</strong>, or activate, the rule in its stated direction.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Order E is marked ready. Do we need another fact to establish packing?\\" options={[\'Yes, we need an additional packing fact.\', \'No, the rule and the ready label establish it.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'The rule already covers every ready order, including E. The separate ready-label fact meets its sufficient condition.\', \'E meets the sufficient condition. With the rule, that is enough to establish that E has been packed.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>We\'ll now keep this job in mind while changing the wording.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={3} label=\\"The sufficient family\\" title=\\"Different words can give you the same connection\\">\\r\\n      <p>An <strong>indicator</strong> is an expression that helps you recognize a conditional relationship. These expressions can introduce an idea that is enough to establish another.</p>\\r\\n      <p>For the next examples, use a different stated rule: anyone who borrows a locker has a key. We will express that same connection in several ways. We haven\'t said everyone with a key borrows a locker.</p>\\r\\n      <WordFamily entries={sufficientFamily} role=\\"sufficient\\"/>\\r\\n      <p>When/whenever and any/anytime group related forms together. An ending changes the kind of case being discussed, but these examples keep the same connection. Read the whole sentence. A familiar word is a clue, not a substitute for its meaning.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Every guest wearing a blue badge receives a lunch voucher. Which complete idea is enough?\\" options={[\'Guest\', \'Guest wearing a blue badge\', \'Receives a lunch voucher\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'Guest alone drops the badge restriction and would make a claim about unbadged guests.\', \'The rule gives a voucher to every guest wearing a blue badge. Keep that qualification with the person.\', \'The voucher is what the rule establishes. It has not said every voucher recipient wears a blue badge.\']}/>\\r\\n      <details className=\\"cr-extension\\"><summary>Two more Group 1 expressions</summary><p><strong>Where</strong> can state a relationship across locations: “Where a collection point operates, parcels can be returned.” An operating collection point establishes the availability of returns there. Availability is not proof that someone made a return.</p><p><strong>The only</strong> needs its complete phrase: “The only notebooks on this shelf are hardback.” A notebook on the shelf is hardback. The sentence does not put every hardback notebook there.</p><p>These are part of your Group 1 work. Understand what the full expression covers before using its group as a placement shortcut.</p></details>\\r\\n      <p>We have seen what can be enough. Now let\'s name what that condition requires.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={4} label=\\"Necessary means required\\" title=\\"The other condition has to be there\\">\\r\\n      <blockquote>{orderRule}</blockquote><p>The <strong>then-part</strong> is the <strong>necessary condition</strong>. Necessary means required. A ready order has to have been packed.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-role-exhibit cr-required\\"><span>Necessary</span><strong>Has been packed</strong><p>Required for an order marked ready</p></div>\\r\\n      <p>Ask “required for what?” Here, required for an order with the ready label. These names describe the roles the conditions have in this relationship.</p>\\r\\n      <p>We\'re looking at the same connection from its other side. The ready label gives us enough to establish packing. Packing is what every ready order requires.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Under our rule, which condition must a ready order meet?\\" options={[\'It has been packed.\', \'It has been collected by the customer.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'Packing is the stated requirement. A ready order that was not packed would violate the rule.\', \'Collection is not part of this rule. The sentence establishes packing, not whether the customer collected the order.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>Necessary does not mean “the next event.” It means required by this relationship. A conditional need not tell you which event caused another, or when either happened.</p>\\r\\n      <p>As with sufficient language, the wording can vary while the relationship stays the same.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={5} label=\\"The necessary family\\" title=\\"Listen for what the sentence needs\\">\\r\\n      <p>Return to our locker rule. Borrowing a locker requires a key. The next expressions all identify that requirement in their complete sentences.</p>\\r\\n      <WordFamily entries={necessaryFamily} role=\\"necessary\\"/>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-contrast\\"><div><h3>If</h3><p>“You borrow a locker <strong>if</strong> you have a key.”</p><p>Having a key is enough for borrowing under this sentence.</p></div><div><h3>Only if</h3><p>“You borrow a locker <strong>only if</strong> you have a key.”</p><p>Having a key is required. This sentence has not made it enough.</p></div></div>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"A guest enters the lounge only if the guest has a current pass. What does entering establish?\\" options={[\'The guest has a current pass.\', \'Every guest with a pass enters.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'Only if identifies the current pass as required for entry. An entering guest therefore meets that requirement.\', \'You made the requirement enough. A guest could have a current pass and remain outside without violating the sentence.\']}/>\\r\\n      <details className=\\"cr-extension\\"><summary>More Group 2 forms, with the sentence intact</summary><p><strong>Only when</strong> and <strong>only where</strong> can restrict the occasions or places of an outcome: “The fountain runs only when its pump is on.” A running fountain requires an operating pump. The pump being on does not establish that the fountain runs.</p><p><strong>Requires</strong> directly names a requirement: “Entry requires a current pass.” Preserve current. <strong>Always</strong> needs the sentence\'s subject and scope: “The upstairs room is always quiet when the door is shut.” Here a shut door establishes quiet, not the other way around.</p><p><strong>Only</strong> and <strong>the only</strong> are different complete expressions. “Only packed orders are marked ready” and “The only orders marked ready are packed” both tell us that a ready order is packed.</p></details>\\r\\n      <p>We can now recognize both roles before writing any symbols. Next, let\'s see what happens when a requirement is missing.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={6} label=\\"A missing requirement\\" title=\\"What if the requirement is missing?\\" dark>\\r\\n      <ContrapositiveDiscovery/>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={7} label=\\"The four situations\\" title=\\"Keep what follows separate from what stays open\\">\\r\\n      <p>Change the fact about one order while keeping the rule. Each fact gives a different starting point. Decide what it establishes before comparing the explanation.</p>\\r\\n      <FourCaseExplorer/>\\r\\n      <p>Starting from packing and concluding ready is the tempting <strong>reverse</strong>. Starting from not ready and concluding not packed is the tempting <strong>inverse</strong>. Neither follows from this rule alone.</p>\\r\\n      <p>The contrapositive starts from <strong>not packed</strong> and establishes <strong>not ready</strong>. Its reasoning depends on the missing requirement, not on reversing whichever words happen to appear.</p>\\r\\n      <p>We now understand the relationship in words. Symbols will let us record that understanding without carrying every word of the sentence.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={8} label=\\"Build the first diagram\\" title=\\"Give the relationship a shorter form\\">\\r\\n      <p>Put the sufficient condition on the <strong>left</strong>, the necessary condition on the <strong>right</strong>, and a <strong>must arrow</strong> between them.</p>\\r\\n      <RuleDiagram left=\\"Sufficient: enough\\" right=\\"Necessary: required\\"/>\\r\\n      <p>The…6622 tokens truncated…       \\"Now compare When I checked the gallery, a lamp was on. That reports what was true on one visit. It hasn\'t said checking the gallery always makes a lamp come on, or that a lamp is on every time someone checks.\\",\\r\\n        \\"When can introduce a rule or a reported occasion. Ask whether the whole sentence gives us what holds whenever the condition is met, or tells us what happened on one particular visit. That meaning comes before the diagram.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      check: {\\r\\n        prompt: \'Which sentence gives a conditional rule rather than reporting one occasion?\',\\r\\n        options: [\'When I checked the gallery, a lamp was on.\', \'Whenever the alarm sounds, the staff evacuate.\'],\\r\\n        correct: 1,\\r\\n        feedback: [\\r\\n          \\"You treated one reported visit as a promise about every visit. The lamp was on when the speaker checked, but the sentence doesn\'t establish a recurring connection between checking and the lamp.\\",\\r\\n          \'Whenever states the recurring connection here: each time the alarm sounds, the staff evacuate. That supplies an exceptionless rule in this sentence; the gallery sentence reports one occasion.\',\\r\\n        ],\\r\\n      },\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'Where: keep the location attached\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"The sentence tells us about a location where a station is available. At that location, availability is enough for the service to operate. Where refers to the station being available, not to service in some unrelated place.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Keep the location the same on both sides. A short label can save writing, but it still needs to refer to the place the sentence concerns.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      prompt: \'A station is available at North Square. What does the rule establish about North Square?\',\\r\\n      reasoning: [\\r\\n        \\"The service operates there. The fact puts North Square in the locations covered by this rule.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Read the diagram as: if a station is available at a location, the service operates there. This fact doesn\'t give us a conclusion about another square whose station status we don\'t know.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'All: name the complete group\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"The statement covers each registered guest. Once you know someone is a registered guest, you can conclude that person receives a wristband.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Registered matters. The target of all is the complete group registered guests, so the sufficient condition includes registration. The rule doesn\'t tell us about every guest regardless of registration.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      prompt: \\"Nora is a guest, but we don\'t know whether she\'s registered. Does this rule settle her wristband status?\\",\\r\\n      reasoning: [\\r\\n        \\"No. The fact doesn\'t yet put Nora in the complete group the rule covers. She could be registered, but we haven\'t been told that.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Keep registered in your label. Guest → Receives wristband would extend the rule to people the original sentence hasn\'t covered.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'The only: read the whole expression\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"The sentence limits the vehicles permitted inside. Every vehicle in that group has to be electric. Start by asking the only what? The target is vehicles permitted inside, not electric vehicles.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Knowing a vehicle is permitted inside is therefore enough to establish that it is electric. The expression\'s complete target has the sufficient role.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      prompt: \'You learn that a vehicle was permitted inside. What does the sentence tell you about it?\',\\r\\n      reasoning: [\\r\\n        \\"It is electric. The rule covers every permitted vehicle, including this one.\\",\\r\\n        \\"The sentence hasn\'t promised that every electric vehicle is admitted. An electric vehicle that remains outside would fit the rule.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      after: [\\r\\n        \\"This is why the only belongs with our sufficient expressions: the complete group it introduces gives us the starting condition. Read it as a whole expression. We\'ll compare it with only once we\'ve learned the other group.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'Every: each qualifying case gets the result\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"Every gives finalist status the same sufficient job that all gave registered-guest status. Pick any person who is a finalist and the sentence settles the invitation question for that person.\\",\\r\\n        \\"The statement doesn\'t tell us who the finalists are. It tells us what has to be true of each one. A separate fact about a person can let us use that connection.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      prompt: \'Someone receives an invitation. Have we established that they are a finalist?\',\\r\\n      reasoning: [\\r\\n        \\"No. Every finalist receives one, but the sentence hasn\'t restricted invitations to finalists.\\",\\r\\n        \\"The rule starts from finalists. It tells you what each finalist gets, not who else might get an invitation. The direction comes from which people the sentence covers, not from which condition seems most important.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'Any: keep the restriction with the person\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"Any covers each applicant who meets the stated restriction. The complete sufficient idea is that the person is an applicant who submits late. Applicant alone doesn\'t capture it.\\",\\r\\n        \\"A fee is paid by any applicant who submits late moves the target later in the sentence. It still tells us what follows for late-submitting applicants. Locate what any refers to rather than using sentence position as a placement instruction.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      prompt: \'Which label preserves the sufficient condition: Applicant, or Applicant submits late?\',\\r\\n      reasoning: [\\r\\n        \\"Applicant submits late. The rule makes that whole condition enough for a fee.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Leaving out submits late changes the statement. It would make every applicant pay a fee, including someone who submitted on time, even though the original sentence hasn\'t said that.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n  ],\\r\\n  \'group-2\': [\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'Only: find who the result is limited to\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"Admission is limited to members. If someone is admitted, the sentence tells us they\'re a member. Only refers to members, and membership has the necessary role.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Ask what the restriction allows you to conclude. Admission tells you membership is present. Membership by itself leaves admission unknown.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      prompt: \'Leon is a member. Does this sentence promise that Leon is admitted?\',\\r\\n      reasoning: [\\r\\n        \\"No. Membership is required, but a member could remain outside without breaking this rule.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Admitted → Member preserves the restriction on admission. Member → Admitted would add a promise about every member that the sentence hasn\'t made.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      after: [\\r\\n        \\"Compare The only people admitted are members. That also tells us every admitted person is a member. The only points to admitted people, the sufficient target. Only members are admitted points to members, the necessary target. Different grammatical targets; the same complete relationship.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'Only if: a condition that must be met\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"The student needs to complete the project for graduation. Only if makes project completion a requirement; it doesn\'t make completion a promise of graduation.\\",\\r\\n        \\"The target is the complete condition completes the project. If graduation occurs, that condition has to be met. That is why it belongs on the required side.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      prompt: \'If my project is completed, does the sentence establish that I graduate?\',\\r\\n      reasoning: [\\r\\n        \\"No. I could complete the project without graduating. The sentence hasn\'t said completion is the only requirement, or that every student who completes the project graduates.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Graduates → Completes project preserves what graduation requires. Reversing that arrow would turn the requirement into a guarantee.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      after: [\\r\\n        \\"Watch what changes when only is added to if below. One sentence makes a pass enough for entry. The other requires a pass for entry. Compare what each one lets you conclude from having a pass.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'Only when: an occasion that is required\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"The sentence restricts reviews to occasions with a filed complaint. A review needs a complaint. Nothing says every complaint produces a review.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Only when a complaint is filed does a review occur moves the required condition to the front. It keeps the same relationship. Find what the sentence requires rather than assuming the first condition goes left.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      prompt: \'A complaint has been filed. Does that alone establish that a review occurs?\',\\r\\n      reasoning: [\\r\\n        \\"No. A filed complaint with no review fits the sentence. The statement restricts reviews to occasions with a filed complaint; it doesn\'t say every complaint produces one.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Review occurs → Complaint filed keeps the required occasion on the right. If we learn that a review occurs, this rule lets us conclude a complaint was filed.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'Only where: keep the requirement at the same place\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"The service needs a station wherever it operates. Only where points to station availability as the requirement.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Compare the Group 1 sentence: Where a station is available, the service operates. That made availability enough. This sentence requires availability for operation. Adding only changes the direction even though both sentences mention the same ideas.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      prompt: \'The service operates at South Square. What must be true there?\',\\r\\n      reasoning: [\\r\\n        \\"A station is available there. Operation at South Square meets the condition the rule tells us about, so availability is required at that same location.\\",\\r\\n        \\"A station somewhere else wouldn\'t satisfy this requirement. Read the diagram as: if the service operates at a location, a station is available there.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'Always: identify what holds in every covered case\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"Read the subject before deciding what always does. This sentence tells us that receiving an invitation holds in every case of someone being a finalist.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Every finalist receives an invitation, so receiving one is necessary for finalist status. Always modifies receives an invitation. A familiar word helps only after we understand its job in the whole sentence.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      prompt: \'What is guaranteed here: an invitation for a finalist, or finalist status for anyone invited?\',\\r\\n      reasoning: [\\r\\n        \\"An invitation for a finalist. The sentence gives one to every person who meets that condition.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Always hasn\'t told us that invitations go only to finalists. The invitation belongs on the right as the result each finalist must receive; starting from it would reverse the relationship.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'Requires: the target can come before the word\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"What does entry require? A current pass. That complete idea is necessary. A pass that has expired doesn\'t meet the condition the sentence gives us.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Now move the requirement: A current pass is required for entry. The pass comes before required, but its role hasn\'t changed. Automatically taking the words after the indicator would point you toward entry and reverse the rule.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      prompt: \'How would you diagram: A current pass is required for entry?\',\\r\\n      reasoning: [\\r\\n        \\"Enters → Has current pass. If someone enters, the required pass is present. The target is a current pass, wherever that phrase appears in the sentence.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Having the pass still doesn\'t guarantee entry. Someone could keep one in a drawer and never enter. Required means needed for the other condition, not enough to establish that it happened.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'Must: preserve an obligation as an obligation\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"Here must states what finalists are required to do. If someone is a finalist, that person has an obligation to attend the interview.\\",\\r\\n        \\"The sentence hasn\'t supplied a fact proving that every finalist complied. Keep required to in the complete target so that your diagram preserves the difference between an obligation and a completed action.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      prompt: \'Maya is a finalist. Which follows: she is required to attend, or she actually attended?\',\\r\\n      reasoning: [\\r\\n        \\"She is required to attend. Maya is a finalist, and the sentence gives every finalist that obligation.\\",\\r\\n        \\"Actual attendance would need information about what Maya did. Finalist → Attends interview would quietly turn the stated requirement into proof of compliance.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n      after: [\\r\\n        \\"Shortening a label should save writing while preserving the claim. Required to attend interview is longer than attends interview, but here those extra words are doing necessary work.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n  ],\\r\\n};\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction IndicatorSections({ id }: { id: string }) {\\r\\n  return <>{indicatorExplanations[id].map((lesson, index) => {\\r\\n    const item = translationExamples[id][index];\\r\\n    return <Section key={item.word} title={lesson.title} expressionNumber={index + 1}>\\r\\n      <blockquote>{item.sentence}</blockquote>\\r\\n      {lesson.paragraphs.map(paragraph => <p key={paragraph}>{paragraph}</p>)}\\r\\n      {id === \'group-2\' && item.word === \'only if\' && <>\\r\\n        <p>Try reading the sentence as though it concerns you. Imagine that you graduate and ask what you now have to know about your project. Then try starting from project completion and see whether the sentence settles graduation.</p>\\r\\n        <p>This is a <strong>Personalized If/Then</strong>. Put yourself in the proposed starting condition, then check what the original sentence requires you to know. We\'re checking its meaning, not predicting what usually happens to graduates.</p>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"If I graduate, what must be true of my project?\\">\\r\\n          <p>I\'ve completed it. The sentence requires project completion for anyone who graduates, including me in this imagined case.</p>\\r\\n          <p>Graduates → Completes project matches that reading. Now try the reverse below.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n      </>}\\r\\n      <ThinkPause prompt={lesson.prompt}>\\r\\n        {lesson.reasoning.map(paragraph => <p key={paragraph}>{paragraph}</p>)}\\r\\n        <Arrow left={item.left} right={item.right}/>\\r\\n        <p className=\\"co-readback\\">{item.readback}</p>\\r\\n      </ThinkPause>\\r\\n      {lesson.after?.map(paragraph => <p key={paragraph}>{paragraph}</p>)}\\r\\n      {lesson.check && <Check {...lesson.check}/>}\\r\\n      {item.word === \'always\' && <div className=\\"co-word-comparison\\"><div><blockquote>A finalist always receives an invitation.</blockquote><p>Start with a finalist. An invitation follows.</p></div><div><blockquote>A person receiving an invitation is always a finalist.</blockquote><p>Start with an invitation recipient. Finalist status follows. Changing the subject changed the rule, even though both sentences contain always.</p></div></div>}\\r\\n      {id === \'group-2\' && item.word === \'only if\' && <DirectionSwitch/>}\\r\\n    </Section>;\\r\\n  })}</>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction Fundamentals() {\\r\\n  return <>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Sufficient means enough\\">\\r\\n        <p>Being marked ready for pickup is enough to know an order has been packed. That makes the ready label <strong>sufficient</strong> for packing. Sufficient means enough.</p>\\r\\n        <blockquote>If an order is marked ready for pickup, it has been packed.</blockquote>\\r\\n        <p>The rule already tells you what has to be true of every order with that label. We call being marked ready the <strong>sufficient condition</strong>. Here, sufficient means enough to establish packing under this particular rule.</p>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"Order C is marked ready. | **Ready order → packed** | Reference stages 1, 2, 4, 6–10; four-case explorer; construction walkthrough; `R/P` notation; reverse/inverse feedback. Opening lesson’s role explorer, Fundamentals, hero, and Group 2 `only` comparison. |
| **Locker borrower → has key** | Both reference word families, fixed role labels, stages 3/5/8, sentence-position comparisons. |
| **Complete folder → signed form** | All four foundation cards plus Group 2 `always`. |
| **Morning tour → map** | Five cards contrasting `if`, `only`, and `only if`. |
| **Shelf mug → blue** | Paired `the only`/`only` cards. |
| **Booking → microphone requirement** | Two cards comparing `requires` and `required` placement. |

Strong candidates for the example-quality review:

- Silver seals proving inspection; complete labels proving signed forms; shelf placement determining color/material: invented sorting policies.
- Kitchen clock triggering oven light; closed drawer required for reading light: unusual mechanisms without intuitive context.
- Locker borrowing requiring a key: assumes a particular locker system.
- Camera borrowing requiring membership; booth use requiring reservations; admission requiring passes: institutional policies, rather than inherent relationships.
- `Must attend` and `must wear` examples intentionally teach obligation versus compliance. Their modality cannot be removed casually.

The Group 1/2 sentence inventories also drive their explanations **by array position**, including exact highlighted spans, feedback, and readbacks. Any later replacement needs to update the whole example family. The 13-stage sequence can remain unchanged.

With the rule, that is enough to establish that you get a bicycle.\']}/>\\r\\n229:      <blockquote>{raffleRule}</blockquote><p>The <strong>then-part</strong> is the <strong>necessary condition</strong>. Winning is enough to establish getting a bicycle. Getting a bicycle is the result the rule requires whenever you win.</p>\\r\\n233:      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Under our rule, what has to follow if you win?\\" options={[\'You get a bicycle.\', \'You ride the bicycle home.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'Getting a bicycle is the stated result.
